title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Stable Graph Classes
authors: Jan Dreier (TU Wien), Ioannis Eleftheriadis (University of Cambridge), Nikolas Mählmann (University of Bremen), Rose McCarty (Georgia Institute of Technology), Michał Pilipczuk (University of Warsaw), Szymon Toruńczyk (University of Warsaw)
abstract: A graph class C is called monadically stable if one cannot interpret, in first-order logic, arbitrary large linear orders in colored graphs from C. We prove that the model checking problem for first-order logic is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically stable graph class. This extends the results of [Grohe, Kreutzer, Siebertz; J. ACM '17] for nowhere dense classes and of [Dreier, Mählmann, Siebertz; STOC '23] for structurally nowhere dense classes to all monadically stable classes. This result is complemented by a hardness result showing that monadic stability is precisely the dividing line between tractability and intractability of first-order model checking on hereditary classes that are edge-stable: exclude some half-graph as a semi-induced subgraph. Precisely, we prove that for every hereditary graph class C that is edge-stable but not monadically stable, first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on C, and W[1]-hard when restricted to existential sentences. This confirms, in the special case of edge-stable classes, an open conjecture that the notion of monadic dependence delimits the tractability of first-order model checking on hereditary classes of graphs. For our tractability result, we first prove that monadically stable graph classes have almost linear neighborhood complexity, by combining tools from stability theory and from sparsity theory. We then use this result to construct sparse neighborhood covers for monadically stable graph classes, which provides the missing ingredient for the algorithm of [Dreier, Mählmann, Siebertz; STOC '23]. The key component of this construction is the usage of orders with low crossing number [Welzl; SoCG '88], a tool from the area of range queries. For our hardness result, we first prove a new characterization of monadically stable graph classes in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs. We then use this characterization to show that in hereditary classes that are edge-stable but not monadically stable, one can efficiently interpret the class of all graphs using only existential formulas; this implies W[1]-hardness of model checking already for existential formulas.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Abstract—A graph class C is called monadically stable if one
cannot interpret, in first-order logic, arbitrary large linear orders
in colored graphs from C . We prove that the model checking
problem for first-order logic is fixed-parameter tractable on every
monadically stable graph class. This extends the results of [Grohe,
Kreutzer, Siebertz; J. ACM ’17] for nowhere dense classes and of
[Dreier, Mählmann, Siebertz; STOC ’23] for structurally nowhere
dense classes to all monadically stable classes.
This result is complemented by a hardness result showing
that monadic stability is precisely the dividing line between
tractability and intractability of first-order model checking on
hereditary classes that are edge-stable: exclude some half-graph
as a semi-induced subgraph. Precisely, we prove that for every
hereditary graph class C that is edge-stable but not monadically
stable, first-order model checking is AW[∗]-hard on C , and W[1]hard when restricted to existential sentences. This confirms, in
the special case of edge-stable classes, an open conjecture that the
notion of monadic dependence delimits the tractability of firstorder model checking on hereditary classes of graphs.
For our tractability result, we first prove that monadically
stable graph classes have almost linear neighborhood complexity,
by combining tools from stability theory and from sparsity theory.
We then use this result to construct sparse neighborhood covers
for monadically stable graph classes, which provides the missing
ingredient for the algorithm of [Dreier, Mählmann, Siebertz;
STOC ’23]. The key component of this construction is the usage
of orders with low crossing number [Welzl; SoCG ’88], a tool
from the area of range queries.
For our hardness result, we first prove a new characterization
of monadically stable graph classes in terms of forbidden induced
subgraphs. We then use this characterization to show that
in hereditary classes that are edge-stable but not monadically
stable, one can efficiently interpret the class of all graphs using
only existential formulas; this implies W[1]-hardness of model
checking already for existential formulas.

We study the model checking problem for first-order logic
on graphs: given a first-order sentence ϕ in the vocabulary of
graphs (consisting of one binary adjacency relation E(·, ·)) and
a graph G, decide whether ϕ holds in G. Arguably, this is the
most fundamental problem of algorithmic model theory, and it
can be used to model many concrete problems of interest. For
instance, the following two sentences express that the graph
in question contains a clique of size k and a dominating set
of size k, respectively.

Clearly, first-order model checking can be solved by bruteforce in time nO(kϕk) on n-vertex graphs, where kϕk denotes
the size of the formula ϕ. In parameterized complexity, the
model checking problem would be called fixed-parameter
tractable if there was an algorithm with a running time of the
form f (kϕk) · nc for a computable function f and constant c.
However, such an algorithm is not expected to exist – a conjecture known as FPT 6= AW[∗] – unless the whole hierarchy of
parameterized complexity classes collapses. Significant effort
has been devoted to the study of restricted classes of graphs for
which first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable,
as well as finding the dividing line between tractability and
intractability. For instance, it is known that the problem is
fixed-parameter tractable on classes of bounded treewidth, by
the seminal result of Courcelle [9] (even for the more powerful
MSO logic), for the class of planar graphs [19], for any class
with bounded maximum degree [34], for classes of bounded
cliquewidth [10], for the class of unit interval graphs [23], and
many others. Despite decades of intensive studies, a complete
classification of the tractable classes is elusive.

A landmark result in this area is the following theorem
due to Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz [24]: If a graph class
C is nowhere dense1 , then the first-order model checking
problem on C can be solved in time f (kϕk, ε) · n1+ε , for
any ε > 0. Here, nowhere denseness is a structural property
of a graph class that turns out to be precisely the dividing
line for subgraph-closed classes: if a subgraph-closed class of
graphs C is not nowhere dense, then model checking on C is
as hard as on general graphs, that is, AW[∗]-hard.

•

However, a complete resolution of Conjecture 1 remains
out of reach for now, due to the insufficient combinatorial
understanding of monadically dependent classes.
It has been long postulated that to approach the tractability
part of Conjecture 1, one should focus first on the simpler
case of monadically stable classes. Here, we say that C
is monadically stable if one cannot interpret arbitrarily long
linear orders in vertex-colored graphs from C . Intuitively,
monadic dependence means that the class in question is not
fully rich from the point of view of first-order logic, whereas
graphs in monadically stable classes are even more restricted:
they are orderless, in the sense that there is no apparent linear
order on any sizeable portion of the graph that could be inferred from its structure. Notably, every nowhere dense graph
class is monadically stable [2], [32], so studying monadically
stable classes already generalizes the setting considered by
Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz [24].

While the result of Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz completely explains the complexity of first-order model checking on subgraph-closed classes, there are natural classes of
graphs that are not nowhere dense where the problem is
still fixed-parameter tractable. Examples include classes of
bounded cliquewidth [10] and, more generally, (some) classes
of bounded twin-width2 [5]. The explanation here is that these
classes are not subgraph-closed, and therefore do not fall under
the classification provided by [24]. Finding a suitable dividing
line for classes that are hereditary — closed under taking
induced subgraphs — remains a central problem in the area.
Around 2016 the following conjecture was formulated. Its
resolution would completely explain the hereditary case.
Conjecture 1 (see e.g. [1], [4], [14], [20]). Let C be a
hereditary class of graphs. If C is monadically dependent,
then first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable
on C . Otherwise, if C is monadically independent, then firstorder model checking is AW[∗]-hard on C .

Stability is a concept studied within model theory for
decades, mostly in connection with Shelah’s classification
theory; see [36], or [38, Chapter 8] for a more basic introduction. Monadic stability was first studied by Baldwin and
Shelah [3] already in 1985, who studied the concept from
the model-theoretic perspective. However, the combinatorial
properties of monadically stable classes have not been studied
until recently in connection with the model checking problem. Dreier, Mählmann, Siebertz, and Toruńczyk [15] and
Gajarský, Mählmann, McCarty, Ohlmann, Pilipczuk, Przybyszewski, Siebertz, Sokołowski, and Toruńczyk [21] obtained
two combinatorial characterizations of monadically stable
graphs classes — through the notions of flip-flatness and of
the so-called Flipper game — which mirror two classic characterizations of nowhere denseness — through uniform quasiwideness [11], [28] and the Splitter game [24]. Particularly,
the Splitter game was one of the two key ingredients in the
fixed-parameter model checking algorithm for nowhere dense
classes of Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz [24]. Very recently,
Dreier, Mählmann, and Siebertz [14] used the Flipper game
to derive fixed-parameter tractability of the model checking
problem on monadically stable classes under the assumption
that a second key ingredient — sparse neighborhood covers
— is also present. Here, a distance-r neighborhood cover of

Here, monadic dependence (also called monadic NIP) is
a notion borrowed from model theory: a graph class C is
monadically independent if one can interpret, in first-order
logic, the class of all graphs in vertex-colored graphs from C ,
and is monadically dependent otherwise. Thus, Conjecture 1,
if true, would provide a magnificent link between model theory
and complexity theory, showing that an important dividing line
studied in one field also fundamentally manifests itself in the
other.

OC ,r,ε (nε ) for any ε > 0 and r ∈ N, where n is

an important subset of monadically stable classes, namely
structurally nowhere dense classes, but the general monadically stable case remained open.
Structurally nowhere dense classes are graph classes which
can be encoded, by means of a fixed first-order formula, in
graphs from a fixed nowhere dense class. For instance, if C is a
nowhere dense graph class, then the class of squares – obtained
by joining vertices at distance exactly two – of graphs in C
is structurally nowhere dense. Those classes are monadically
stable, and it is conjectured [22], [30] that the two notions
coincide (see the discussion below). There are examples of
graph classes that are known to be monadically stable but are
not known to be structurally nowhere dense. Those include
classes of bounded local shrubdepth and edge-stable classes
of almost bounded twin-width or flip-width [39].

Our two main results are fueled by three contributions of
independent interest. First, we show that monadically stable
graph classes have almost linear neighborhood complexity.
Second, we give a new characterization of monadic stability in
terms of forbidden induced subgraphs, and finally, we prove
a logical hardness result concerning classes which are not
monadically stable. We now explain these results and how
they are used.

A. Contribution
In this work we construct sparse neighborhood covers in
general monadically stable graph classes, and thereby prove
that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable
on every monadically stable graph class. We also prove a
complementary hardness result which shows that in the setting
of hereditary classes that are edge-stable — exclude a halfgraph as a semi-induced subgraph4 — monadic stability is precisely the dividing line delimiting tractability and intractability
of first-order model checking. The following two statements
describe our main results formally.

The proof of Theorem 2 proceeds in two steps. The first
step is to prove that monadically stable classes have almost
linear neighborhood complexity, as explained formally in the
theorem below.
Theorem 4. Let C be a monadically stable graph class and
ε > 0. Then for every G ∈ C and A ⊆ V (G),
|{NG [v] ∩ A : v ∈ V (G)}| ⩽ OC ,ε (|A|1+ε ).
In the language of combinatorics of set systems (and closely
related to the Vapnik-Chervonenkis, or VC, dimension [40]),
Theorem 4 says that set systems of neighborhoods in graphs
from monadically stable classes have near-linear shatter functions. The proof of Theorem 4 relies on a reduction to the case
of nowhere dense classes, for which the statement is known
to hold [18]. This reduction exploits both sampling techniques
in the spirit of ε-nets, and the concept of the branching index
(or Shelah’s 2-rank), which is a crucial tool in the study of
stable theories within model theory.

systems and VC-dimension: orders with low crossing number
due to Welzl [41]. In a nutshell, Welzl proved that under

for every n-vertex graph G ∈ C , the vertices of G can be
linearly ordered so that the neighborhood of every vertex is

B. Discussion
We discuss the relationship of our work in the context of
other work in the area.
We first discuss our proof of Theorem 2, and its ingredients.
Dreier, Mählmann, and Siebertz [14] established the fixedparameter tractability of the model checking problem for all
structurally nowhere dense classes (which are included in
monadically stable classes, and the two notions are conjectured
to coincide). There are three main ingredients of their result,
similarly as in the proof of Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz [24]
achieving the same for nowhere dense classes:
1) the Flipper game, which was obtained in [21], and yields
a tree-like decomposition of the considered graph, albeit
whose size is too large to be handled by an fpt algorithm;
2) sparse neighborhood covers, which – using the method
of [24] – allow one to replace the tree-like decomposition
by one of fixed-parameter tractable size;
3) a dynamic programming algorithm processing the treelike decomposition, based on locality of first-order logic.

results concerning nowhere dense classes. On the other hand,
monadically stable graph classes are – by definition – those
which do not encode large half-graphs using a first-order formula. Unlike in the case of structurally nowhere dense classes,
we cannot rely on the existence of any known underlying
structure; the feat is precisely to reveal some sort of global
underlying structure. As far as we know, Theorem 4 is the first
known nontrivial structural, quantitative7 statement that holds
for all monadically stable classes, among the multiple similar
statements that are known to hold for nowhere dense classes
and structurally nowhere dense classes. Indeed, the almost
linear neighborhood complexity (as described in Theorem 4)
was shown to hold in structurally nowhere dense classes
already in [31]. To prove this for monadically stable classes,
we introduce a new technique for reducing the monadically
stable case to the nowhere dense case; see Proposition 9.
Next, we discover a direct link between almost linear neighborhood complexity and the existence of sparse neighborhood
covers. The construction of neighborhood covers in nowhere
dense classes [24] relied on weak coloring orderings, which
are crucial in the study of sparse graphs. The construction in
structurally nowhere dense classes [14] also ultimately relied
on weak coloring orderings in nowhere dense classes (via socalled quasi-bushes [13]). An analog of weak coloring orderings in the dense setting is missing and highly desired [39].
Our key observation is that weak coloring orderings can be
replaced by Welzl’s orders with low crossing number, allowing
us to construct sparse neighborhood covers in a novel, and
remarkably simple manner (see Lemma 12).
As an illustration of its power, this observation, together
with the almost linear neighborhood complexity in structurally
nowhere dense classes [31], immediately implies item 2)
above – the existence and efficient computability of sparse
neighborhood covers in structurally nowhere dense classes –
replacing a 30-page-long argument from [14].
Apart from its simplicity, our method of constructing
neighborhood covers is efficient and can be executed in
time O(n5 ), while the construction from [14] relied on a
slower approximation algorithm based on rounding an LP
relaxation. Consequently, we improve the running time of the
previous algorithm for model checking [14] from OC ,ϕ (n11 )
to OC ,ϕ,ε (n6+ε ), for any ε > 0.

bounded diameter. We view this as a first step towards the
conjecture [22], [30] that monadically stable graph classes
coincide with structurally nowhere dense graph classes. As
a next step, we propose a weaker variant of this conjecture
(see [12]). Our conjecture was confirmed very recently by
Braunfeld, Nešetřil, Ossona de Mendez, and Siebertz [7],
using the structural properties of the neighborhood covers

Perhaps more importantly, our proof of Theorem 4 and the
actual construction of neighborhood covers feature powerful
ideas from the theory of VC dimension, in particular the
concept of orders with low crossing number due to Welzl. We
anticipate that these tools – which are not limited to monadically stable classes – will play an increasingly important role
in the emerging theory of monadically stable and the more
general monadically dependent classes. In particular, Welzl
orders with low crossing number, and sparse neighborhood
covers, exist in all monadically dependent classes, assuming
those have almost linear neighborhood complexity, which we
pose as Conjecture 13.
We now discuss our lower bound, Theorem 3, and its main
ingredients: Theorem 6, which characterizes monadically stable graph classes in terms of forbidden induced substructures,
and Theorem 7, which encodes all graphs in those patterns
using existential formulas. Both results seem to be of independent interest, as they lead to further corollaries beyond the
immediate scope of this work. For instance, in the full version
[12] we demonstrate this, by showing that in the context of
Shelah’s classification programme in model theory, the notion
of NSOP (Not the Strict Order Property) collapses to monadic
stability, for hereditary graph classes. Recently, a subset of the
authors developed a characterization of monadically dependent
graph classes that generalizes Theorem 6, from which they
subsequently derived the hardness part of Conjecture 1 [16].
Both the Ramsey arguments and the hardness result in [16]
have their roots in the present work. The latter result is based
on a different method of “deobfuscating” flips than the one
used in this work. The method of [16] is simpler, but has the
drawback of not relying only on existential formulas, so it
does not give hardness of existential model checking. In this
work we take the extra mile to derive the stronger hardness
results described in Theorem 3.
Finally, our forbidden pattern characterization (Theorem 6)
and the logical hardness result (Theorem 7) are combinatorial
strengthenings of logical characterizations of monadically stable classes from [6] (which apply more generally to relational
structures).

In this extended abstract, we sketch the key ideas behind
the proofs of our main results. We first give some short
preliminaries in Section II. Then in Section III, we establish structural properties of monadically stable graph classes
– almost linear neighborhood complexity (Theorem 4) and
sparse neighborhood covers (Theorem 5) – and derive the

25

fixed-parameter tractability of the model checking problem
(Theorem 2). In Section IV, we study classes that are not
monadically stable, show that they exhibit certain regular
patterns (Theorem 6), and derive logical hardness (Theorem 7)
and computational hardness (Theorem 3). Finally, in Section V, we draw conclusions and give an outlook on the area.
All of the proofs sketched in this overview are given in
detail in the full version of this paper [12]. A complete proof
of the model checking result, including the full algorithm, can
also be found in the PhD thesis of one of the authors [26].

III. S TRUCTURE SIDE
We borrow the terms structure side and non-structure side
from model theory, specifically, Shelah’s classification theory [36].
The premise of classification theory is that there
exist true dichotomies, called “dividing lines” so
that models of theories that lie on the “good” side
of a dividing line can be analyzed in some way (and,
more generally, possess many “nice” properties),
whereas the theories on the “dark side”, that is,
on the other side of the dividing line, admit various
kinds of non-structure. [37]
In our case, the dividing line is monadic stability, and the
structure side (that is, every monadically stable class) enjoys
various good properties, such as the characterization via Flipflatness [15], or via Flipper games [21]. In this section, we
exhibit further properties of monadically stable classes, which
have a quantitative aspect. In Section IV we explore the nonstructure side of the dichotomy, by exhibiting some “wild”
properties of classes that are not monadically stable.

For a finite set of unary predicates L, an L-colored graph is
a structure consisting of a graph and, for every predicate in L,
a subset of vertices satisfying the predicate. Interpretations
can be naturally generalized to colored input graphs, while
producing uncolored graphs on output. A transduction consists
of a finite set of unary predicates L and an interpretation I
mapping L-colored graphs to graphs. For a transduction T =
(L, I) and a graph class C , we define the image of T on C
as T(C ) := I(C L ), where C L is the class of all L-colored
graphs whose underlying (uncolored) graph belongs to C .
A graph class C transduces a graph class D if there
exists a transduction T such that D ⊆ T(C ). Transducibility
is a transitive relation on graph classes. We say that C is
monadically dependent if C does not transduce the class of
all graphs. The class C is moreover monadically stable if C
does not transduce the class of all half-graphs. (Recall from an
earlier footnote that a half-graph Hn of order n is the bipartite
graph with sides {a1 , . . . , an } and {b1 , . . . , bn } where ai
and bj are adjacent if and only if i ⩽ j.) As mentioned in
Section I, we say that C is edge-stable if there exists some
n ∈ N such that no graph in C contains Hn — the halfgraph of order n — as a semi-induced subgraph. Thus any
monadically stable class is edge-stable, for otherwise we could
color the vertices on either side of the semi-induced halfgraph with two different colors and remove edges between
vertices of the same color in order to transduce the class of
all half-graphs. Finally, C is structurally nowhere dense if
some nowhere dense graph class transduces C .

By Theorem 6 and hereditariness, it suffices to consider two
cases: C either contains a k-flip of every r-subdivided clique
or a k-flip of every r-web, for some fixed k, r ⩾ 2. The two
cases differ in their technical details; nonetheless, the general
proof strategy is the same for both, and so we only highlight
the case of subdivided cliques. Up to increasing the value
of r by a constant factor, we may ensure by hereditariness
that C also contains a k-flip of every r-subdivided biclique:
an r-subdivision of a complete bipartite graph. While a simple
graph gadget argument reveals that every class that contains
all non-flipped r-subdivided bicliques existentially interprets
the class of all graphs, we only know that C contains kflips of those. The main challenge therefore lies in definably
“reversing” the flips. Using Ramsey’s theorem for bipartite
graphs, the pigeonhole principle, and hereditariness, we conclude that C contains for each r-subdivided biclique a kflip that is in a certain sense canonical. Moreover, for each
canonical flip, the flip partition P is minimal in the sense
that no two parts can be merged. Given a canonical k-flip of
an r-subdivided biclique, the key to reversing the flip is to
recover for every vertex v its part P(v) in P. From here, a
rather naive strategy proceeds by existentially quantifying a
representative vertex zi for each part Pi ∈ P, checking the
adjacency between v and a realization to zi to see whether
P(v) was flipped with Pi , and finally determining P(v) using
minimality of the flip partition. However, this approach runs
into problems as the realization of each quantified vertex zi
does not necessarily lie within Pi . To overcome this, we
instead quantify a small set Zi of representatives for each part,
and check whether v is connected to the majority of Zi . Using
the structural properties of subdivided bicliques, we then argue
that this allows us to approximately recover P(v), up to parts
that behave symmetrically. This is sufficient to definably tell
which pairs of vertices were flipped.
This provides us with a way to recover the unflipped edge
relation of a subdivided clique within its k-flip. Building
up from the edge formula, we obtain for every existential
formula ϕ an existential formula flip(ϕ) such that ϕ is true in
a subdivided clique if and only if flip(ϕ) is true in its k-flip
present in C .

In this work we prove that first-order model checking is
fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically stable class of
graphs. Moreover, monadic stability turns out to be the dividing line between tractability and intractability on edge-stable
classes of graphs, which verifies Conjecture 1 on such classes.
Indeed, Theorem 3 establishes the AW[∗]-hardness of the
model checking problem on all hereditary, edge-stable graph
classes which are not monadically dependent. This result, and
